code.title: Walk the class loader chain

followUps:
Override loadClass so it tries its own findClass first and only falls back to super.loadClass when that fails. To keep it safe, always delegate java.* and the shared API packages (for example servlet-api) to the parent, so nobody can replace String and types crossing the boundary stay the same Class.

synchronized (getClassLoadingLock(n)) {
  Class<?> c = findLoadedClass(n);
  if (c == null && !n.startsWith("java.")) {
    try { c = findClass(n); } catch (ClassNotFoundException e) { }
  }
  if (c == null) c = super.loadClass(n, false);
  return c;
}

It is the loader a thread hands to library code so that code can find classes it cannot see itself. JDBC's DriverManager or ServiceLoader live in a parent loader, yet must create your driver from the application's loader, so they call Thread.currentThread().getContextClassLoader(). A container sets it per request to the web-app loader.

Pitfall: if you change it on a pooled thread, restore it in finally.

It happens because the two Cart classes were loaded by two different loaders, and class identity is (name, defining loader), so they are unrelated types. Typical case: Cart sits in both a shared lib folder and the WAR, or a hot-reload loader reloaded it while old instances survive.

Diagnose by printing obj.getClass().getClassLoader() and Cart.class.getClassLoader(). Fix by keeping one copy in the parent, or sharing an interface loaded by the parent.

code.title: ExceptionInInitializerError then NoClassDefFoundError

followUps:
The class is marked as failed forever. The first use throws ExceptionInInitializerError wrapping the real cause. Every later use throws NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class X, without the original stack trace, and the JVM never retries the initializer.

So in logs always search for the first ExceptionInInitializerError: that is the real bug. Example: a static field reading a missing config file fails once at startup, then thousands of NoClassDefFoundErrors follow.

Shading copies a dependency into your jar (often renamed) so it cannot clash, but two different versions of the same library can still end up loaded. Code compiled against the newer API calls a method that the older copy on the classpath does not have, so linking fails with NoSuchMethodError at runtime. Example: compiled against Guava 31, but Guava 19 wins on the classpath.

Find the winner with mvn dependency:tree and -verbose:class, then align versions or relocate packages.

code.title: When does a static block run?

followUps:
Yes. Class initialization holds a lock, so two threads can wait on each other. Thread 1 initializes class A whose static block touches B, while thread 2 initializes B whose static block touches A: each waits for the other's init to finish, and neither ever does.

class A { static int x = B.y + 1; }
class B { static int y = A.x + 1; }
// T1: A.x   T2: B.y   -> possible deadlock

Avoid cross-class static dependencies and never start or join threads inside a static block.

Because static final String S = "hi" is a compile-time constant: javac copies the literal straight into the calling bytecode, so there is no getstatic and the class is never touched. A static final List is not a constant expression, so reading it needs the field value, which forces initialization and runs the static block.

Constants must be primitives or Strings initialized with constant expressions; Integer.valueOf(5) is not one.

code.title: A tiny operand stack machine

followUps: They are invokestatic, invokevirtual, invokeinterface, invokespecial and invokedynamic. Static methods use the first; ordinary class methods dispatch through the vtable with invokevirtual; interface methods use invokeinterface; constructors, super.m() calls and (before Java 11) private methods use invokespecial; lambdas and modern string concatenation use invokedynamic, linked by a bootstrap method on first call.

javac moves the lambda body into a private synthetic method such as lambda$main$0 and emits an invokedynamic instruction. On the first execution the JVM calls LambdaMetafactory, which generates a hidden class implementing the functional interface and links the call site to it. Later calls are fast, and a non-capturing lambda is created once and reused. No separate .class file exists for it, unlike an anonymous inner class.

It is the class-file format version, which equals the Java release plus 44: 52 is Java 8, 61 is Java 17, 65 is Java 21. A JVM runs class files up to its own version only; an older JVM loading a newer file throws UnsupportedClassVersionError. Check a file with javap -v Foo.class, and set the output with javac --release 17.

code.title: Monomorphic vs megamorphic call site

followUps:
A call site is megamorphic when it has seen three or more receiver types, so C2 cannot inline it behind a cheap type guard and falls back to a vtable or itable call. Without inlining it also loses escape analysis and other optimizations, so hot loops can be several times slower.

Example: a loop calling shape.area() over Circle, Square and Triangle. Fixes: keep call sites to one or two types, sort or split loops by type, or use a switch over a sealed type.

Both attack slow start-up, in different ways. Recent JDKs (Project Leyden) add an AOT cache that saves loaded and linked classes, and later profile data, from a training run, so start-up and warm-up are faster but the JIT still runs. GraalVM native image compiles the whole program ahead of time: instant start and low memory, but a closed world, reflection must be declared, and there is no runtime JIT to reach peak optimization unless you use profile-guided builds.

The JIT stops compiling: the log prints "CodeCache is full. Compiler has been disabled" and newly hot methods stay in the slow interpreter, so throughput falls off a cliff. The default reserved size is about 240 MB with tiered compilation. Check usage with jcmd <pid> Compiler.codecache, and raise -XX:ReservedCodeCacheSize if it is genuinely needed, or find code generation that keeps creating classes.

code.title: Non-escaping vs escaping allocation

followUps:
Pooled objects live a long time, so they get promoted to the old generation, and each write of a young reference into them triggers card-marking work. They also escape, so escape analysis cannot remove them, and you pay for reset logic and thread-safety. Meanwhile a fresh allocation is just a TLAB pointer bump and a young GC only pays for survivors.

Pool only genuinely expensive things: connections, threads, large direct buffers.

Run the benchmark with -prof gc and read gc.alloc.rate.norm, the bytes allocated per operation. If allocation was eliminated, it is about 0 B/op; a surviving Point shows its size (for example 24 B/op). Confirm by making the object escape (store it in a field or pass it to a Blackhole) and seeing the number jump, or by comparing with -XX:-DoEscapeAnalysis.

code.title: Stack frames vs heap data

followUps: Start the JVM with -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary, then run jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary. It splits usage into heap, class, thread, code, GC, symbol and internal. Take baseline first and later summary.diff to see growth. It costs a few percent overhead. Compare the total with RSS from pmap or container metrics: the gap is native malloc by libraries the JVM cannot track.

PermGen was a fixed-size area that held class metadata, controlled by MaxPermSize, and it was hard to size, so "OutOfMemoryError: PermGen space" was common. JDK 7 moved interned strings to the heap and JDK 8 (JEP 122) replaced PermGen with Metaspace, which lives in native memory and grows on demand. Cap it with MaxMetaspaceSize; class loader leaks now eat native memory instead.

With a heap under about 32 GB the JVM stores object references in 32 bits, scaled by 8-byte alignment (2^32 x 8 = 32 GB), which is called compressed oops. Beyond that every reference becomes 8 bytes, so a 32 GB heap can hold less than a 28 GB one. Example: 10 million references cost 40 MB compressed and 80 MB uncompressed.

Stay below about 31 GB, or jump well past it (40+ GB). Check -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal | grep UseCompressedOops.

code.title: Mark phase from GC roots

followUps: The danger is the application changing references while the collector marks, so a live object could be missed. Collectors use barriers to prevent this. G1 and Shenandoah use a SATB pre-write barrier that records the old value before it is overwritten, so everything reachable when marking began stays marked. ZGC uses load barriers that check and fix pointers when they are read. CMS used a post-write barrier to re-scan changes. Short stop-the-world phases handle the roots.

The card table is an array with one byte per 512-byte card of the old generation. When code stores a reference into an old object, a write barrier marks that card dirty. A minor GC then scans only dirty cards to find old-to-young references, rather than the whole old generation. Cost: one small store per reference write. G1 uses per-region remembered sets for the same purpose.

code.title: Minor GC: survivors, ages and promotion

followUps: Run with -Xlog:gc+age=trace. Premature promotion shows as a survivor age table whose computed tenuring threshold drops from 15 to 1, plus old-gen occupancy that grows after every young GC even though the live set is small, and full or mixed GCs that become frequent. Example: threshold 15 falling to 1 means survivors overflow. Fix by enlarging survivor or young space, or by allocating fewer medium-lived temporaries.

A bigger young generation means fewer minor GCs and more time for objects to die, so fewer survive each collection. Pause time depends on survivors, not on young size, so pauses often stay the same or shrink. Example: at 500 MB/s allocation, a 1 GB Eden collects every 2 s, a 100 MB one every 0.2 s. Costs: less memory for old gen, and if a lot of data is live (large caches) each pause gets longer.

ZGC runs out of free memory because it cannot reclaim it as fast as the application allocates, so the allocating thread stalls until a cycle frees space. The log shows "Allocation Stall", and requests pause for milliseconds to seconds. Remedies: a bigger heap, more concurrent GC threads, or a lower allocation rate. Stalls mean the headroom is too small, not that ZGC is broken.

G1 treats the goal as a target: it shrinks the young generation to fit, so GCs run far more often, objects have less time to die, and more of them are promoted early. Mixed GCs also evacuate fewer old regions per pause, so the old generation fills up and G1 may fall back to a Full GC lasting seconds. A 10 ms goal can therefore raise the worst pauses. Use a realistic goal (100 to 200 ms) or switch to ZGC.

With fewer than 2 CPUs or under about 1.8 GB visible memory, the JVM does not count as a server-class machine and picks Serial GC. So a 1-CPU pod gets Serial even with 4 GB of memory. Check with -Xlog:gc+init or -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal | grep Use.*GC. Either give the pod at least 2 CPUs or select the collector explicitly, e.g. -XX:+UseG1GC.

code.title: G1 region size and humongous objects

followUps: Add -Xlog:gc* and look for "G1 Humongous Allocation" as the GC cause. Fix: raise -XX:G1HeapRegionSize (e.g. 16m) so the objects fall below half a region, or stop creating huge temporaries by streaming in chunks, reusing buffers and pre-sizing collections. Example: with 2 MB regions a 1.5 MB array is humongous; with 8 MB regions it is a normal Eden allocation. Find the allocating code with JFR allocation events.

SATB means Snapshot-At-The-Beginning: concurrent marking treats every object that was reachable at the start of the cycle as live. Before the application overwrites a reference, a pre-write barrier saves the old target in a queue. Without it, the app could delete the last path to an unvisited object after moving the reference into an already-scanned object, and the marker would miss a live object. Price: floating garbage until the next cycle.

code.title: Find a GC-shaped p99 spike

followUps: Then the stall is probably not a GC pause. Suspects: a long time-to-safepoint (a counted loop delays the stop), CPU throttling by the cgroup quota (check nr_throttled in cpu.stat), swapping, a noisy neighbour, a slow disk blocking log writes, lock contention, or thread-pool starvation. Use -Xlog:safepoint, JFR safepoint events and OS metrics to separate them.

Measure the live set after a full GC, then size heap at 3 to 4 times that, and the pod limit at heap plus non-heap memory. Example: live set 800 MB gives a 3 GB heap; add about 1 GB for metaspace, threads, code cache and direct buffers, giving a 4 GiB limit. Use -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70 rather than a fixed -Xmx, set memory request equal to limit, and verify RSS under load.

code.title: Unbounded cache leak vs bounded LRU

followUps: Shallow size is the memory of the object alone (header plus fields); retained size is everything that would be freed if that object were collected, meaning all objects it alone keeps alive. Example: a HashMap object has about 48 bytes shallow, but with 1 million entries it may retain 80 MB. In Eclipse MAT sort the dominator tree by retained size to find the real culprits.

Only its keys are weak; the values are held strongly by the map. If a value references its own key (or the key is reachable elsewhere), the entry never becomes collectable. Keys that are interned strings, literals or cached Integers also never die, and entries are cleaned lazily on later map access. Example: map.put(key, new Holder(key)) leaks forever.

A dump pauses the application for as long as it takes to write 30 GB (minutes) and needs that much disk. Take it from one replica removed from the load balancer, and consider jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump -gz=1 file to compress. Without -all only live objects are dumped, after a full GC, which shrinks it. Try JFR's Old Object Sample first, and analyse on a machine with enough RAM for MAT.

code.title: Match a hot thread id to a jstack nid

followUps: Because the JVM reports a thread that is blocked in native network I/O as RUNNABLE, even though it uses no CPU. A dump full of RUNNABLE threads in socketRead0 therefore points at idle waiters, not at the CPU burners. Use per-thread CPU time (top -H, or the cpu= field in a dump) to find actual consumers, and a wall-clock profile when the problem is latency.

Profilers that sample through safepoints can only see a thread when it reaches a safepoint poll, which sit at method returns and non-counted loop back-edges. So time gets credited to the nearest poll, not the real hot code, and tight counted loops may not show up at all. Profilers such as async-profiler and JFR sample with signals at any instruction, so they avoid the bias.

Record with JFR, then open the file in JDK Mission Control (Memory, Allocations) or aggregate jdk.ObjectAllocationSample events, which carry a sampled stack trace and a weight. Group by top frame and by class: the biggest weights are the hot spots. Sampling is throttled, so overhead stays low.

jfr print --events jdk.ObjectAllocationSample rec.jfr
jfr summary rec.jfr

Then remove or shrink the top allocation site and re-measure.

Use jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json file.json (JDK 21). Plain jstack lists only platform threads, so it hides the virtual threads. JFR also reports jdk.VirtualThreadPinned events, which show where a virtual thread blocked its carrier thread. The JSON dump groups threads by thread container, which makes it practical for thousands of threads.

code.title: Sizing heap for a 4 GiB pod

followUps: A CPU limit is a CFS quota per 100 ms period. A pod limited to 2 CPUs gets 200 ms of CPU time per period across all threads. A parallel GC with several worker threads plus app threads can burn that quota in a few milliseconds, and then the whole container is frozen until the next period. A 20 ms pause becomes 100 ms of wall time. Check nr_throttled in cpu.stat, then raise the limit or lower GC thread counts.

A virtual thread keeps its stack as objects on the heap that grow and shrink with use, so an idle one costs a few hundred bytes to a few KB, not a reserved 1 MB native stack. The budget therefore moves from thread stacks to the heap: 100,000 virtual threads may need only some hundreds of MB of heap, plus GC work to scan them. Only the carrier threads (about one per CPU) still use native stacks.
